7.text: Each family has a special place for the sacrifice to the dead, which is

8.text: in the cemetery, and is called “hearth enclosure” (pênuˊkwun). If, during the

9.text: ceremony, there are close by corpses of those who have died recently, various

10.text: precautions are taken. Some of those who are sacrificing bring harpoons

11.text: and lances, and use them as if stalking the dead, and striking them with

12.text: their weapons. Others bring thongs, and spread slings before the corpses.

13.text: After finishing the ceremony, the people repeat their hostile demonstrations

14.text: and then run away in a most hurried manner.

15.text: Among the Maritime people it often happens that persons die at sea

16.text: whose bodies are never recovered. Those who have perished in this manner

17.text: receive a special sacrifice offered at the very edge of the water. In the

18.text: feast, the share of the dead is thrown into the water. One and the same

19.text: place on the shore serves for all commemorative sacrifices of this kind, and

20.text: each family has two “hearth enclosures” in which to offer them, — one in

21.text: the village cemetery for those who died on land; and another on the shore,

22.text: close to the water, for those who perished at sea.

23.text: A man who is supposed to have perished at sea, but who in the end

24.text: escapes and lands on shore, must undergo a purifying ceremony. For this

25.text: he is girded with a piece of thong. Then a dog is sacrificed to the sea,

26.text: on the shore. After that the man is taken to the refuse-heap used by his

27.text: family, where he must lie down on the ground and wallow in the rubbish.
